passage.title: The Vault of Wild Seeds
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
Walk through a modern wheat field and you will see millions of stalks standing at the exact same height. Farmers breed food crops for big yields, sweet taste, and smooth harvest by machine. Yet planting a single uniform crop across vast plains carries a hidden risk. Because every stalk shares the same traits, a single new fungus or insect pest can sweep through and wipe out the whole harvest. When farm crops lose their natural defenses, where can scientists find the traits needed to save them?

A century ago, a Russian plant scientist named Nikolai Vavilov found the answer high in rugged mountain ranges. Travelling by mule across five continents, he noticed that wild cousins of wheat, corn, and potatoes still grew in the hills where farming first began. Unlike pampered farm plants, these tough wild weeds had battled drought, frost, and rot for thousands of years. Each harsh valley forced the local plants to keep rare traits that helped them survive.

Vavilov realized that these ancient birthplaces, which he called centers of origin, held a priceless treasure for human food. If a new blight struck modern farm wheat, breeders could crossbreed that weak crop with a wild mountain cousin that could shrug off the mold. To guard those traits before wild valleys were plowed under, he built the world's first seed bank in Leningrad. Across five continents, thousands of wild seed packets were gathered by Vavilov before modern plows cleared the old hills. By the 1930s, his vault held more than two hundred thousand distinct samples of grains, beans, and tubers.

Preserving a seed vault takes far more than locking tin boxes inside a cool stone basement. Seeds are living embryos that slowly lose their power to sprout if they sit on a shelf for decades. Every few years, staff must plant a portion of each sample in guarded test plots, harvest fresh seeds, and dry them for cold storage. During the harsh siege of Leningrad in World War II, Vavilov's team guarded the vault day and night so future crops would not perish.

Today, global vaults buried in Arctic ice still follow the blueprint that Vavilov drew a hundred years ago. Whenever scorching heat or a strange rust mold threatens the world's bread supply, plant breeders turn to those cold shelves. Inside a single rough seed from a mountain weed may rest the exact code needed to feed the next century.

tier2Words.definition: All the same in form, size, or appearance, with no variation
tier2Words.contextClue: Millions of wheat stalks stand at the exact same height and share the exact same traits.

tier2Words.definition: A plant disease caused by fungi or bacteria that withers and kills crops
tier2Words.rootHint: An old agricultural word for a sudden withering disease on leaves and grain
tier2Words.contextClue: When a crop disease strikes farm wheat, breeders look for a wild cousin that can shrug off the mold.

tier2Words.definition: Clearly different and separate from others of the same kind
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'distinguere' meaning to separate or mark apart
tier2Words.contextClue: The seed vault held more than two hundred thousand separate, unique samples of grains and beans.

tier2Words.definition: To die, be destroyed, or pass away completely
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'perire' meaning to pass away or be lost
tier2Words.contextClue: Scientists guarded the seed collection during the siege so future food crops would not die out.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Across five continents, thousands of wild seed packets were gathered by Vavilov before modern plows cleared the old hills."

Who performed the action of gathering the wild seed packets in this sentence?

options.text: The modern plows that cleared the old hills
options.childFeedback: Watch out—'before modern plows cleared the old hills' only tells when the seeds were collected in Paragraph 3, not who gathered them.

options.text: The thousands of wild seed packets
options.childFeedback: Careful—this choice flips the action! The thousands of wild seed packets were what got gathered, not who did the gathering.

options.text: Vavilov, the Russian plant scientist
options.childFeedback: Spot on! In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by Vavilov' right after 'were gathered' shows that the Russian scientist Vavilov collected the seed packets.

options.text: The farmers who planted uniform wheat across the plains
options.childFeedback: Watch out—modern plains farmers appear in Paragraph 1, whereas Paragraph 3 states the wild seeds were gathered by Vavilov.

questions.provingSentenceText: Across five continents, thousands of wild seed packets were gathered by Vavilov before modern plows cleared the old hills.
questions.childTip: Spot on! In Paragraph 3, the phrase 'by Vavilov' right after 'were gathered' shows that the Russian scientist Vavilov collected the seed packets.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'thousands of wild seed packets' is the receiver of 'were gathered.' The agent phrase 'by Vavilov' identifies who performed the gathering.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 3, find the action phrase 'were gathered' and check the noun right after 'by' to see who collected the packets.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 1:

"Yet planting a single uniform crop across vast plains carries a hidden risk."

What does the word "uniform" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Identical and lacking variety from plant to plant
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 1 explains that millions of stalks stand at the exact same height and share the same traits, showing that 'uniform' means identical and lacking variety.

options.text: Grown high on rugged mountain slopes
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 2 contrasts the uniform plains crops with the wild cousins that grow high on rugged mountain slopes.

options.text: Protected against every kind of insect pest
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 1 states the exact opposite: because uniform stalks share the same traits, a single insect pest or fungus can wipe them all out.

options.text: Dressed in heavy winter work clothes
options.childFeedback: Watch out—while 'uniform' can mean work clothes in other settings, here it describes wheat stalks that all share identical plant traits.

questions.provingSentenceText: Yet planting a single uniform crop across vast plains carries a hidden risk.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 1 explains that millions of stalks stand at the exact same height and share the same traits, showing that 'uniform' means identical and lacking variety.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 describes stalks standing at the exact same height and sharing the exact same traits, showing that 'uniform' means identical and lacking variation.
questions.retryHint: In Paragraph 1, look at the sentences right before and after: millions of stalks stand at the exact same height and share the same traits.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 4, why must seed bank workers periodically plant a portion of their stored seeds in test plots?

options.text: Farmers buy all the stored seeds from the vault every spring to feed their mules.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 3 mentions Vavilov riding mules on collecting trips, not farmers feeding vault seeds to mules.

options.text: Wild mountain seeds turn into ordinary farm wheat if they stay inside tin boxes.
options.childFeedback: Careful—staying in foil packets does not turn wild seeds into farm wheat; Paragraph 4 says old seeds simply lose their ability to sprout.

options.text: Arctic ice melts every summer and floods the stone basement of the vault.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 4 explains that cold vaults keep seeds dry and freezing, with no mention of melting ice flooding the underground rooms.

options.text: Stored seeds are living embryos that slowly lose their power to sprout on a shelf.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that even in cold storage, living seed embryos slowly lose their power to sprout over decades, so workers must grow fresh replacements.

questions.provingSentenceText: Seeds are living embryos that slowly lose their power to sprout if they sit on a shelf for decades.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 4 explains that even in cold storage, living seed embryos slowly lose their power to sprout over decades, so workers must grow fresh replacements.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 4 explains that because seeds are living embryos that lose viability over decades, workers must periodically grow them out in test plots to harvest fresh seeds.
questions.retryHint: Look in Paragraph 4 for the sentence that explains what happens to living seed embryos if they sit on a shelf for decades.

questions.prompt: Which evidence does the author provide to support the claim that wild crop cousins are crucial for protecting the modern food supply?

options.text: Wild mountain weeds produce much larger yields and sweeter grain than modern farm wheat.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraphs 1 and 2 state the opposite: modern farm crops are bred for big yields and sweet taste, while wild weeds have small, bitter grains.

options.text: Wild plants survived drought, frost, and rot, keeping hardy traits breeders can cross into farm crops.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that wild mountain plants survived drought, frost, and rot, preserving tough traits that breeders can cross into modern food crops.

options.text: Modern harvesting machines can only cut stalks that grow in rugged mountain valleys.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 1 explains that farmers grow uniform crops on flat plains specifically so machines can harvest them smoothly.

options.text: A single packet of wild seeds can be ground into enough flour to feed a whole city.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 5 explains that wild seeds hold genetic traits to save future harvests, not that one packet makes enough flour to feed a city.

questions.provingSentenceText: If a new blight struck modern farm wheat, breeders could crossbreed that weak crop with a wild mountain cousin that could shrug off the mold.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraphs 2 and 3 explain that wild mountain plants survived drought, frost, and rot, preserving tough traits that breeders can cross into modern food crops.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraphs 2 and 3, the author supports the claim by showing that wild relatives evolved natural resistance to drought, frost, and rot, which breeders can crossbreed into vulnerable farm crops.
questions.retryHint: Connect what wild weeds endured in Paragraph 2 with how breeders use them to fight blight in Paragraph 3.

questions.prompt: Part A: Why are modern farm fields more vulnerable to being wiped out by a single disease than wild mountain valleys?

options.text: Wild mountain valleys are sprayed every week by plant breeders from Arctic seed vaults.
options.childFeedback: Careful—Paragraph 2 explains that wild mountain plants survive on their own through natural variety, not because breeders spray mountain valleys.

options.text: Modern farmers refuse to water or fertilize their wheat fields once the stalks sprout.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—the passage never claims modern farmers refuse to water their fields; the risk comes from every plant being genetically identical.

options.text: Fungi and insect pests can only survive on flat plains and never enter mountain ranges.
options.childFeedback: Watch out—Paragraph 2 specifically mentions soil rot and harsh conditions in mountain valleys, proving pests and diseases exist there too.

options.text: Every stalk shares identical traits, so a disease that harms one plant can harm them all.
options.childFeedback: Spot on! Paragraph 1 explains that because every stalk in a modern field shares the exact same traits, a single fungus or pest that harms one plant can wipe out the whole crop.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because every stalk shares the same traits, a single new fungus or insect pest can sweep through and wipe out the whole harvest.
questions.childTip: Spot on! Paragraph 1 explains that because every stalk in a modern field shares the exact same traits, a single fungus or pest that harms one plant can wipe out the whole crop.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 1 explains that genetic uniformity makes modern crops vulnerable: when every plant shares identical traits, one fungus or pest can destroy the entire harvest.
questions.retryHint: Look at Paragraph 1 for the sentence that explains the danger of every stalk sharing the same traits.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Farmers breed food crops for big yields, sweet taste, and smooth harvest by machine."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains why farmers like uniform crops, not why those fields are easily wiped out by disease.

options.text: "Because every stalk shares the same traits, a single new fungus or insect pest can sweep through and wipe out the whole harvest."
options.childFeedback: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 1 directly proves Question 5 by showing how shared traits let a single fungus or pest destroy the entire harvest.

options.text: "By the 1930s, his vault held more than two hundred thousand distinct samples of grains, beans, and tubers."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this detail from Paragraph 3 only tells how many seed samples Vavilov collected by the 1930s.

options.text: "Today, global vaults buried in Arctic ice still follow the blueprint that Vavilov drew a hundred years ago."
options.childFeedback: Not quite—this concluding line from Paragraph 5 praises Vavilov's legacy rather than explaining why uniform farm fields are vulnerable to disease.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because every stalk shares the same traits, a single new fungus or insect pest can sweep through and wipe out the whole harvest.
questions.childTip: Spot on! This quote from Paragraph 1 directly proves Question 5 by showing how shared traits let a single fungus or pest destroy the entire harvest.
